extracted.intended_audience: college-level students who write and peer-review essays (including tutors and writing-center users)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for students to both receive and give constructive peer reviews of college essays, including a step-by-step review process, reviewer qualities, and a 10-question checklist for assessing drafts against assignment criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting reviews / be teachable
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach suggestions with the right attitude: be teachable, humble, and willing to learn from others to improve your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put aside defensive reactions so you can consider ideas for revision with an open mind. Treat suggestions as opportunities to learn, not as attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand evaluation vs. judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that instructor feedback in draft stages is often evaluative and suggestive rather than a final judgment or grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't read formative feedback as final—use it to guide revisions. Instructors often intervene after outlines/first drafts with forward-looking commentary rather than a quantitative judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peers' ideas are suggestions; author decides
rubrics_metrics.description: Peers may offer ideas that add value or may not fit your plan; their input is advisory and the final decisions belong to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If peers are part of your intended audience, their suggestions may be especially valuable. If not, seek outside readers from the target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tutors effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: If consulting a tutor, ensure the tutor understands the assignment and bring a clear copy of the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have specific questions prepared. Don't expect tutors to 'fix' your paper; they advise—final responsibility for revisions rests with you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer qualities: focus, prioritize author, provide specific feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should remain focused on improving the text, prioritize the needs of the author, and provide specific, insightful feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think critically about how well the text fulfills its purpose in the rhetorical situation; keep suggestions concrete and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal attacks and do not hijack the text
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus critique on how the text presents argument and fulfills purpose rather than attacking the author, and avoid imposing your own stance or changing the author's purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the author's intended stance and purpose in mind; do not suggest revisions that fundamentally change those without clear justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize revision issues: content first
rubrics_metrics.description: When a draft is not final, reviewers should prioritize issues in this order: content, focus, organization, topic, and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because drafts will be revised, detailed grammar and spelling corrections are less useful than substantive comments about argument and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground critiques in the text
rubrics_metrics.description: Good reviewers offer insight grounded in the text: point out inconsistencies, question logic, seek clarification, and identify assumptions the author may have taken for granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific passages/examples when pointing out problems or suggesting changes to make feedback actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Step 1 — Read the paper through completely
rubrics_metrics.description: First, read the paper all the way through to appreciate what the writer is trying to say before making comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the main point is unclear, read a second time. Remember you act as part of the essay's audience—ensure you 'get it' before critiquing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Step 2 — Compare to assignment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold the paper up against the assignment's criteria: identify the writer's main point and check whether the draft fulfills the assignment requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (ad analysis): look for a clear thesis naming strategies used by the advertiser, strong ad description, discussion of magazine context, and analysis with examples. Ask: does the writer fulfill the criteria?

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Step 3 — Provide at least three positives and three improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the writer feedback containing at least three positive comments and at least three areas the writer could improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specific examples and concrete suggestions (e.g., tell how to 'spice up' the introduction rather than only saying it's weak). Offer reasons to help the author choose revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Step 4 — Include recap, likes, and improvement areas; be respectful
rubrics_metrics.description: Your review should include a recap of the main point, three things you like about the paper, and three areas it could be improved, communicated with respect and consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the 'golden rule': help the author improve without putting them down. Balance constructive criticism with encouragement; don't only praise when there are clear improvements needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Step 5 — Focus on revision over proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize revision-level feedback (structure, argument, evidence, focus) rather than editing or proofreading for grammar and mechanics in a draft stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save line-editing and copyediting suggestions for later drafts unless errors obscure meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious questioning factual content
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing content, remember the author may know more about the topic—don't challenge facts unless you're reasonably certain they're incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid suggesting changes simply because you'd write it differently; only recommend changes you believe will make the essay stronger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specific examples when suggesting changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When pointing out weaknesses, include specific examples and concrete ideas for revision rather than vague comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., instead of 'intro lacks luster', offer phrasing, hooks, or structural changes that would improve the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — What does the writer do well?
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and articulate the strengths of the essay (what the writer does well).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give reasons for praise so the author knows which aspects to preserve during revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — What needs work?
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the key weaknesses or problem areas in the essay that the writer should address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize and be specific so the author can tackle the most important issues first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — Introduction: attention and thesis linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the introduction grab attention and lead smoothly to a thesis? If not, suggest improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer ways to strengthen the lead and make the transition to thesis clearer and more engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — Paragraph unity and topic sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Does each paragraph develop one main idea and do topic sentences tie back to the thesis?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out paragraphs that try to do too much or whose topic sentences don't connect to the central argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — Evidence and persuasiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the writer offer evidence for points in each paragraph, and is the evidence convincing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note where evidence is missing, weak, irrelevant, or needs better integration or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — Transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the essay use transitions between paragraphs and ideas to ensure flow?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest specific transitional phrases or structural reorganizations to improve coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — Conclusion effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the conclusion briefly summarize the main argument in a fresh way and end on a memorable note (quotation, image, call to action)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the memorable impression the conclusion leaves and, if weak, suggest ways to make it more striking or conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — Formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the essay formatted correctly (margins, font, spacing, etc.) according to assignment or style requirements?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify any formatting corrections needed and point to the assignment's formatting expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — Grammar, spelling, and citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there grammar and spelling errors, and are MLA/in-text citations done correctly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note major mechanical errors that affect clarity; cite specific examples and, if relevant, point out citation/format problems to fix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist — Final overall thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer any additional final thoughts that don't fit other categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this space for overarching suggestions about scope, voice, audience fit, or next steps for revision.
